title: The Black Death
hookLine: plague sweeps Europe; some priests flee, others stay to bury and bless

lines: THE PESTILENCE THAT WALKETH IN DARKNESS.
WHO WILL COME TO THE SICK?
cards: "Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness." That's from Psalm ninety-one in the King James Bible, a psalm about trusting God when danger is everywhere.
In the Middle Ages, a pestilence walked through the towns of Europe in broad daylight. A sickness that came fast, with fever and swellings. Whole households emptied.
Markets closed. Graveyards filled, and then there wasn't room. People ran from the cities if they could.
And in town after town the same question arrived at the church door: who will come to the sick? Who will hear their last words, and bury them?

teach.b: People wrote it down while it was happening, and the writers of the time describe priests, doctors and neighbors facing a choice. Some fled.
It's hard to blame them; the sickness spread from person to person, and staying could mean dying.

teach.h: SOME STAYED TO NURSE AND BURY.
teach.b: But some stayed. Priests went into houses where the sick lay, to hear confession, to anoint, to give the last communion. Monks and nuns nursed people they didn't know.
Townspeople carried the dead to be buried when no family was left. Some who stayed caught the sickness and died themselves. Why stay?

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: The answer goes back to the scene we met with Elizabeth of Hungary, the sheep and the goats in Matthew, where the king also says to the righteous, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me".
Whatever they did for the least of these, they did for him.
Catholic tradition gathered acts like these into a list called the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, and also burying the dead, which comes from the book of Tobit.
Protestant churches place Tobit outside their canon, but kept the same command to visit the sick from Matthew. So the plague years hold two stories side by side.
One is terror, and flight, and blame, and real cruelty toward people treated as outsiders. The other is quieter, and shorter to tell. Some stayed.

how: Christians remember the plague years when they pray for the sick and for those who care for them, and Catholic Christians still teach visiting the sick and burying the dead among the works of mercy.

games.q: you're a priest in a town where the plague has arrived. people are dying in their houses, and the sickness spreads by contact. what do you do?
o: leave for the countryside until it passes.
stay, and go into the houses of the sick.
lock the church and pray from inside.
games.why: some fled, and the writers of the time say so. but some stayed to hear confession, anoint and bury, and some of them died too.

practice: Let the people who stay with the sick come to mind one by one: a nurse finishing a night shift, a doctor making one more call, someone cleaning a hospital room, a chaplain at a bedside, a family member who has given up sleep.
If you know one of them by name, let that face come. If you pray, pray for their strength and rest; if not, hold them in your thoughts, and let gratitude sit with them.
